prompt: Win rate 45% (hypothetical). What is the probability of three losses in a row, starting at a given trade, in percent? Assume independent trades.
After five losses in a row, a trader says: 'I am due a win.' Which response is correct?

options.text: Yes. The average must be restored, so the next trade is more likely to win.
No. If trades are independent, each trade has the same chance of a win whatever happened before.
Yes, because the market always corrects a long run of losses.
No, because after losses the chance of a win falls.

explanations.a: This is the gambler's fallacy. Past losses do not change the chance of the next trade under the independence assumption.
explanations.c: Markets have no obligation to correct a run. A long run of losses is an outcome, not a debt.
explanations.d: Under the independence assumption, the chance does not fall after losses. Saying it falls is also a mistake, though a different one.

prompt: Spot the mistake. Statement: 'My win rate is 60% (a). So I will win at least one of the next five trades (b). The chance of five losses in a row is 0.4^5, about 1%, so the chance of at least one win is about 99% (c).' Which part is wrong?

options.text: So I will win at least one of the next five trades.
The chance of five losses in a row is about 1%, so the chance of at least one win is about 99%.

explanations.a: This is the stated win rate of the hypothetical plan. It is a frequency, not a promise for the next trades.
explanations.c: This is correct under the independence assumption. 1 - 0.01024 = 0.98976, which is about 99.0%. It is a probability, not a certainty.

prompt: Your written rule: pause trading after five losses in a row. You have lost four in a row at 1% risk. The next trade is taken and loses. What does the rule say?

options.text: Double the size on the next trade to recover faster.
Pause, because the fifth loss in a row is the trigger the rule sets.
Keep trading at 1%, because the rule only applies after ten losses.
Drop the rule, because losses are random and the rule does not apply.

explanations.a: Increasing size after losses is not allowed. It breaks the capital-first rules and is a martingale-style method (T6.5).
explanations.c: The rule says five. Changing the threshold after the fact is a judgement made during a loss, which the rule was written to prevent.
explanations.d: A rule written before a streak is there for the streak. Dropping it during a loss is the failure the rule is meant to stop.

prompt: Five losses in a row prove my system is broken. Which statement is correct?

options.text: Yes. Five losses in a row is conclusive.
No. Streaks happen at some frequency, and one streak on its own is not evidence that the system has stopped working.
Yes, if the same streak happens twice in a month.
No, because a broken system never has a losing streak.

explanations.a: A streak is one short run of outcomes. It is not conclusive on its own, and the number of trades behind it matters.
explanations.c: Repeat streaks are still streaks. Judge the system on expectancy with a sample size, not on how often bad runs appear.
explanations.d: A broken system can have losing streaks, and a working system can have them too. Streaks do not separate the two on their own.
